data.title: Trump, Xi and Putin's 'peace declaration' leaves out the wars in Iran and Ukraine
data.description:
Takeaways from the historic summit between Trump, Xi and Putin

ELAINE KURTENBACH, KANIS LEUNG and AAMER MADHANI
Updated Thu, November 19, 2026 at 3:43 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin on Thursday was the first-ever sit-down for the leaders of the three countries.

They started with talk of a shared responsibility for keeping peace as the victors of World War II and as global powers. But post-meeting readouts by the three nations reflected more symbolism than substance.

The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran. It said they agreed on the need for reforms to the United Nations, on increasing oil supplies and on reducing nuclear risks. The statement did not spell out the type and extent of the U.N. reforms the leaders agreed to.

Advertisement

The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, opposing what they called "jurisdiction abuse" by the International Criminal Court, the reports said.

Here are key takeaways from the talks, which lasted over an hour.

China's Xi presided over the summit of 21st century powers

Xi added to China's already burgeoning diplomatic stature merely by hosting the event.

He said the talks with Trump and Putin were positive and fruitful, and that the three nations had aligned views on safeguarding world peace, according to China's Xinhua official news agency.

They agreed major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously and believe differences should be resolved through negotiation and cooperation, Xinhua reported.

"As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace," Xi was quoted as saying. "The seeds planted at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit."

China's insistence that it has the right to recover the democratically governed island of Taiwan, possibly by force, was not addressed in the leaders' broadly worded agreement. China considers that a domestic issue.

China likes to position itself as a different kind of superpower from the U.S. and Russia — one that doesn't get involved in wars and advocates for smaller states, said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.

Beijing's priority was steering the meeting away from specifics, she said. "Beijing wanted to be seen as the adult in the room."

Trump claims a place in history

Trump heralded the leaders' gathering as "really making history" and he suggested to Xi and Putin that together they were shaking things up by ditching the "old school" way adversaries engage.

The White House set low expectations for the talks. But Trump framed them Thursday as only the beginning — a chance to get the conversation rolling on solving some of the world's thorniest issues.

"A lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start," Trump told Putin during a one-on-one meeting prior to their three-way meeting with Xi.

The carefully crafted event was a welcome break for Trump after a couple of rotten weeks for his presidency in which his Republican Party was trounced in the midterm elections, widespread tech outages spooked Americans, and Iran escalated attacks on U.S. allies.

Trump said Iran was on the agenda. China and Russia carry enormous sway with Tehran and also have been accused by the U.S. of supporting the Islamic Republic.

He reiterated Thursday that he and Xi agree Iran needs to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for world energy supplies that has become a chokepoint since the start of the war. They also agree that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon, Trump said.

But there were no signs that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.

Putin shares spotlight with Trump and Xi

For Putin, the three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit — and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier — offered a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to signal that he heads a superpower on par with the United States and China.

Trump and Putin found common ground in their opposition to the ICC. The Russian leader is wanted by the ICC under an arrest warrant for his alleged war crimes in Ukraine. The U.S. opposes the ICC's arrest warrant against former Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Putin last attended an APEC summit in 2017. His presence as an honored guest and Russia's status as a top global power — at least at the gathering in Shenzhen — mark a diplomatic breakthrough.

Just before the summit, Russia sent a pair of nuclear-capable Tu-95 bombers on a visit to Vietnam in a reminder of its nuclear might. And as Putin arrived in China, Russian TV zeroed in on an officer in his retinue who was carrying a briefcase with the codes for Moscow's nuclear forces.

Putin addressed Xi as "dear friend" during their talks on Wednesday, and smiled contentedly on Thursday as he shook hands with Trump, who called him "my friend" and boasted about their "great relationship for many years."

Speaking at the start of the three-way talks, Putin underscored the global weight of Russia, China and the U.S. The three nations are "united not only by our status as victors in World War II, but, most importantly, by our shared responsibility for maintaining international peace and security," he said.

They are also among the founders of the United Nations, Putin noted, adding that "we bear responsibility for preserving and strengthening the system of international law."

"Our nations share many common interests regarding the resolution of regional conflicts, including, of course, the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said.

Russia's war in Ukraine featured in Putin's bilateral meetings with Trump and Xi. It wasn't the main topic of the three-way talks, Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

The Kremlin released video of the Chinese leader escorting the Russian president to his car at the end of the talks and the two men shaking hands.

"I don't think anyone even expected things to go so well," Putin told Xi as the two men parted ways.

___

Madhani reported from Washington and Leung reported from Hong Kong.

data.title: Sen. Elissa Slotkin fires back at DOJ official over investigation of her political speech
data.description:
FIRST ON NBC NEWS
Congress
Congress

Sen. Elissa Slotkin fires back at DOJ official over investigation of her political speech

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz has suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Nov. 18, 2026, 8:33 PM EST
By Ryan J. Reilly

WASHINGTON — A Democratic senator repeatedly targeted by the Trump administration for potential prosecution due to her political remarks is firing back at a Trump-appointed Justice Department official over what she called a “baseless” inquiry into her rhetoric about congressional oversight.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is one of five Democratic members of Congress who have been the subject of letters that the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, has posted on social media. In one of the letters, which have come under scrutiny from legal experts, Reitz suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight potentially acting as a “deterrence message” to people considering joining the Trump administration could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.

“I made those statements consistent with my basic right to freedom of speech, a right that every American enjoys under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” Slotkin wrote Wednesday in a letter to Reitz obtained by NBC News. “In addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility.”

“The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts,” she wrote. “As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.”

Slotkin went on to say that Reitz’s “public threats” violated Justice Department policy, and that his decision to publicly post the letter rather than providing it to her, her attorney or the Senate legal counsel “is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”

Reitz, 39, previously worked as chief of staff for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and became U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas over the summer after placing fourth in the Republican primary for state attorney general.

Reitz also posted letters on X to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.

He told NBC News this week that he was “not interested in chilling free speech.”

Slotkin and five other sitting Democratic lawmakers were separately targeted by the Trump administration earlier this year over a video they posted to social media that sought to remind members of the military and intelligence communities that they should not obey unlawful orders. Allies of the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, tried to indict the six Democrats for their speech in that video, but federal grand jurors unanimously rejected the indictment attempt.

Slotkin’s attorney, Preet Bharara, had previously written a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche cautioning him against following President Donald Trump’s public instruction to look into Slotkin’s political speech, which he dubbed a “criminal act.”

Blanche has conceded that Slotkin’s words alone were “absolutely not a crime” and said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.”

data.title: Denmark unanimously approves Greenland security deal with the U.S.
data.description:
Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland, hoping to end conflict

By Stine Jacobsen and Tom Little
Thu, 19 November 2026 at 1:22 pm UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Vote on the security agreement between Denmark, Greenland, and the USA in the Parliament Hall, Copenhagen

1 of 4
A session on ratifying a security agreement with US President Donald Trump covering Greenland takes place in the Danish parliament in Copenhagen, Denmark, November 19, 2026. REUTERS/Tom Little

By Stine Jacobsen and Tom Little

COPENHAGEN, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Denmark's parliament on Thursday unanimously ratified a security agreement with the United States on Greenland, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's ‌future that has rattled transatlantic relations.

The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September after US ‌President Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich self-governing Danish territory of 57,000 people.

Advertisement

The executive agreement takes effect once Denmark's foreign ​ministry tells the US in a diplomatic note that procedures are complete. It does not need approval from the US Senate.

It expands the US military's role in Greenland, including permission to establish a "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.

The signatories will now start work on a new Greenland law to screen outside investors on security ‌grounds and plans for two new US ⁠military bases, as outlined in the agreement, Denmark's Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus told Reuters.

"I expect that the US will now also start to be more concrete on the purposes and ⁠the arrangement around these two areas," he said Bruus.

Advertisement

Trump's refusal to rule out military or economic force to acquire the island triggered a diplomatic crisis within NATO in January and months of intensive negotiations.

DIFFICULT TIME FOR GREENLANDERS

Naaja Nathanielsen, a Greenlandic member of the ​Danish ​parliament, said Trump's pressure had led to distrust in Greenland ​towards the US administration.

"It's been really difficult for ‌Greenlanders these past two years. It's been seeping into every aspect of our lives," Nathanielsen told Reuters. She hoped the agreement would open a path to dialogue after hurtful rhetoric within the Western alliance.

Advertisement

The US ambassador to Denmark, Kenneth Howery, welcomed the vote result, calling the agreement "a tremendous accomplishment" that bolsters the security of all sides, including NATO.

Greenland's parliament ratified the deal this month. Danish lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalize the situation in ‌Greenland.

Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor at the University ​of Copenhagen said the deal was more likely a beginning than an ​end.

"With the treaty in hand, the US will ​be able to demand greater influence on decisions that have security policy implications and on ‌part of the extraction of strategic resources," he ​said.

Advertisement

Other experts say the new ​agreement does not add much US military access to Greenland. The northernmost US base is already in Greenland, which lies on the shortest route from Europe to North America.

Trump last month said that "massive oil, gas ​and mineral exploration" was set to ‌begin on Greenland, a contentious statement on a territory that has banned new drilling for crude. ​Denmark has said any resource extraction must respect local law.

(Reporting by Stine Jacobsen, editing by Jacob ​Gronholt-Pedersen, Louise Rasmussen, Rod Nickel, Thomas Derpinghaus and Chizu Nomiyama )

data.title: Denmark unanimously approves Greenland security deal with the U.S.
data.description:
Denmark ratifies Trump deal over Greenland

By Stine Jacobsen and Tom Little
Thu, November 19, 2026 at 9:14 AM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Stine Jacobsen and Tom Little

COPENHAGEN, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Denmark's parliament on Thursday unanimously ratified a security agreement with US President Donald Trump ‌covering Greenland, hoping to end a standoff over the Arctic island's future that ‌has rattled transatlantic relations.

The US, Denmark and Greenland signed the agreement in September to resolve tensions after ​Trump repeatedly threatened to take control of the mineral-rich island, a self-governing Danish territory that is home to 57,000 people.

Advertisement

The deal was backed by 109 Danish lawmakers and none voted against, the parliamentary tally showed.

The deal is not subject to a vote by the ‌US Senate. The executive agreement ⁠will, following Thursday's vote in Copenhagen, enter into force once the Danish foreign ministry informs the US in a diplomatic note that ⁠procedures are complete.

The deal expands the US military's role in Greenland, including permission to establish a "Golden Dome" missile defence system, while reaffirming Danish sovereignty and Greenlanders' right to self-determination.

Trump's refusal ​to rule ​out military or economic force to acquire ​the island triggered a diplomatic crisis ‌within NATO in January and forced Denmark and Greenland into months of intensive negotiations.

Greenland's parliament ratified the deal this month. Last week, it passed a first reading in Denmark's parliament with backing from all parties, and lawmakers expressed relief and hope that the deal will normalize the situation in Greenland.

"However, there are many indications that this ‌is not an end, but rather a beginning," ​said Mikkel Vedby Rasmussen, a political science professor ​at the University of Copenhagen.

"With ​the treaty in hand, the US will be able to demand ‌greater influence on decisions that have ​security policy implications and ​on part of the extraction of strategic resources," he said. Other experts say the new agreement does not add much US military access to Greenland.

The ​shortest route from Europe to ‌North America runs via strategically located Greenland, where the northernmost US ​military base is already located.

(Reporting by Stine Jacobsen, editing by Jacob Gronholt-Pedersen, ​Louise Rasmussen, Rod Nickel and Thomas Derpinghaus)

data.title: Trump praises Putin ahead of rare three-way meeting with Xi in China
data.description:
Politics

Trump, Xi, Putin set for rare joint meeting in China

By
Joe Walsh
Senior Editor, Politics
Joe Walsh is a senior editor for digital politics at CBS News. Joe previously covered breaking news for Forbes and local news in Boston.
Read Full Bio
Joe Walsh

Updated on: November 19, 2026 / 1:57 AM EST / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

President Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin are about to hold talks in Shenzhen, China, a rare face-to-face meeting among the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries.  

Before that gathering, Mr. Trump met separately with Putin, and then Xi.

The U.S. president and Putin spoke on the sidelines of China's Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

"We've had a great relationship for many years," Mr. Trump said while standing alongside his Russian counterpart. "I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start."

Cameras captured Mr. Trump, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent entering a small conference room in Shenzhen to meet with Putin, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov and other Russian officials. 

As Mr. Trump approached Putin for a handshake, he said, "Who is that?" before laughing and saying, "He's my friend."

Russia's TASS news agency said the war in Ukraine was the main topic they discussed, and that Putin left the meeting in "an excellent mood."

Mr. Trump then met for about an hour with Xi ahead of the three-way gathering. As the session began, Xi told Mr. Trump relations between China and the United States are "stable and improved."

Mr. Trump told reporters he spoke with Xi for two hours on the APEC sidelines Wednesday, with trade and tariffs the main topics. He also noted he would be asking China to "do some more" for American farmers, because China has an "insatiable appetite."

He said he intends to discuss ending the Ukraine war with Xi and Putin.

Mr. Trump has said previously that he planned to talk about denuclearization with the leaders of China and Russia which, along with the United States, make up the world's three largest holders of nuclear weapons.

But a range of other global challenges are lingering in the background, including the war in Iran and tensions over trade and artificial intelligence.

The summit is taking place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed, is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing. 

Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

Mr. Trump brought up AI during a speech at the APEC forum earlier in the day, vowing to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.

"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."

Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.

Mr. Trump said in his APEC speech the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.

During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.

Foreign conflicts loom large during the Trump-Putin-Xi talks. Iran is one contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.

The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."

Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island, which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."

And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported. Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

data.title: 'There was no monitoring': Sources dispute FAA oversight of work before ground stop
data.description:
Passengers wait at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA), in Arlington, Virginia, just outside Washington, DC, on November 14.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

On the morning of last week’s historic nationwide ground stop, an FAA technician escorted a private contractor from L3Harris into a remote radio communications site for air traffic control centers in south Arkansas, to replace a decades-old router.

The FAA technician believed his role ended when the contractor entered the facility. He went about his own work without knowing exactly what the L3Harris engineer was doing, according to two sources familiar with what happened in the room, and the union that represents FAA technicians.

Not long after it was replaced, that new router triggered a cascade of communications problems, flooding the FAA’s aging network with data and leading the FAA to take the rare step later that day of issuing a full nationwide ground stop. About 3,500 planes were in the air when departures were halted for more than four hours while the agency worked to figure out the problem.

The details of how that router was installed and who was overseeing that work is now in dispute and emerging as a key point of tension in unraveling what exactly went wrong that day.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford has defended the FAA’s modernization process and insisted that the L3Harris engineer performing the upgrade “was monitored by an FAA technician” and that a risk assessment was done beforehand.

But sources who spoke to CNN dispute this characterization. The technician “was only there to unlock the door,” one of them said.

“There was no monitoring,” another source said.

That kind of hands-off arrangement, sources say, is a recent development and represents a stark change from how this kind of maintenance work was handled by previous administrations, when the FAA typically exercised far more oversight of contractors’ work.

A crucial memo from March 2025

But in an effort to speed up and streamline the modernization of the nation’s air traffic control system with $12.5 billion from President Donald Trump’s “big beautiful bill,” the administration diminished FAA oversight of this kind of work, the sources said.

In a memo dated March 2025, the FAA laid out some key changes to how maintenance and upgrades would be carried out, noting: “It is critical to approve maintenance performed by the Telecommunication Vendors without delay.”

Under the policy change, the FAA shifted from receiving maintenance “requests” from its private contractors to receiving “notifications” of intended work, noting that “this work will proceed without FAA approval,” according to the memo.

Airplanes are parked on the tarmac after the US Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop "due to extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety" following the agency's earlier report of serious air traffic control communications issues at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, on November 13.

The memo does note that an FAA liaison will evaluate the “purpose, severity, criticality and impact” of the work, but the sources told CNN there are only a handful of liaisons nationwide processing thousands of notifications.

“So what level of oversight are they really doing?” one of the sources said.

As a result, the L3Harris contractor at the center of Friday’s outage showed up with just a few days’ notice and conducted the work without any meaningful oversight from the agency, according to the sources and the union.

The March 2025 memo “laid the groundwork for what happened last Friday,” the source said.

“They’re not requesting to go out anymore. They’re just notifying and going and then they’re doing the work,” the source said. “And that circumvents the operational risk management aspect where the technician before who works for the government could say, no, no. You can’t do that right now.”

Elizabeth Doherty, a spokeswoman for the Professional Aviation Safety Specialists union that represents FAA technicians, told CNN the technician’s “orders were to simply let the contractor in the building,” that he “had no direction to help or assist in any way,” and that “no PASS-represented employee was asked to conduct a risk assessment on this particular upgrade.”

CNN asked the FAA about the discrepancy over whether an FAA technician was or was not providing real time oversight of the work.

“There is a lot of information that we’re trying to track down. So things have been changing,” FAA spokeswoman Hannah Walden told CNN by phone. “It could have been a misunderstanding or whatever. So I’m not saying one way or the other right now. I just am saying we’re trying to provide information as we get it.”

In addressing the changes laid out in the 2025 memo, Walden denied oversight has been reduced, saying the policy change “does not change oversight at all. It changes the priority of the work that needs to be done.”

The episode underscores the complications that can arise over a communications system that is operated by the federal government yet is owned by a private company, in this case L3Harris, whose telecom network serves as the communications backbone for the nation’s airspace.

It also comes as Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is asking Congress to approve another $50 billion to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control system even as lawmakers question how the billions allocated last year were spent.

L3Harris declined to provide any details in response to CNN’s questions.

In a statement to CNN, the company said it is “supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel.”

People sit on the floor as they wait to try and retrieve luggage during delays and cancellations at LaGuardia airport on November 13, 2026 in the Queens borough of New York City.

A routine job, then chaos

The policy change laid out in the March 2025 memo didn’t come out of nowhere. The sources familiar with what happened before the ground stop said a chronic, yearslong shortage of FAA technicians as well as the Trump administration’s push for speed helped propel it forward.

The result, they believe, was less oversight of the contractor on Friday and a much slower recovery, as the FAA struggled to pinpoint the source of the problem.

L3Harris notified the FAA on November 9 that it planned to carry out maintenance, replacing a router, at a remote FAA facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, with work set to begin at 9 a.m. on Friday, November 13, one of the sources said.

Four days after the notice, the L3Harris worker arrived.

Even the time of day the work was scheduled raised eyebrows, given it was at a time of heavy air traffic. The sources say FAA technicians were not consulted about the best time to carry out this work at this facility.

By that Friday afternoon, the new router was connected and the L3Harris contractor had left the site with no idea of the chaos that was beginning to unfold, the source said.

Hours later, FAA technicians got a call telling them to return to the site to escort the L3Harris engineer back into the facility. The agency scrambled to find the closest available staff to let him in. Hours had passed between the time the engineer had left and the time he returned to retrieve the router, the source said.

A former FAA technician told CNN that, for agency technicians, checking in with air traffic controllers before leaving a site is standard practice. It’s not clear if the L3Harris engineer took this step.

“As a technician, anytime when I was out there … and I did anything, anything at all to the equipment before I left, I would call up the TRACON or the center or the tower, whatever controllers that had the services that I was providing on that equipment. And I would say, ‘I’m getting ready to leave. Everything look good? Everything okay? You got everything?’ They’d be like, ‘yep,’” the former technician said. “It’s just a practice that you do.”

In the immediate aftermath of the ground stop, Duffy was sharply critical of L3Harris, making a point of calling them out in his public remarks.

“We need L3Harris or whoever provided that router to us to do a better job,” Duffy said during his Saturday press conference. “Many of our contractors, many or our partners, they take our money and they provide really poor service to us. Full stop.”

Yet by Tuesday, Bedford sounded a different tone toward L3Harris.

At a news conference, Bedford described the L3Harris contractor who replaced the router as a “highly trained certified engineer, former Air Force veteran, I’m told a generally competent guy doing the work that he has done dozens and dozens of times before.”

Asked what oversight the FAA provides when contractors work at FAA facilities, Bedford also said, “There is a comprehensive risk management process with every installation. And that installation happens whether it’s with a contractor or with an FAA employee.”

Days earlier, Duffy had defended the timing of the work, pointing out that it was at a remote location. He said he didn’t expect the kind of impact seen last Friday at “smaller locations.”

data.title: Republicans want Trump to confront Xi over 2 Americans accused of spying
data.description:
Lawmakers urge Trump to press Xi on detained Americans, political prisoners

By Simon Lewis and Jonathan Landay
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 10:48 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

US President Donald Trump arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the APEC Leaders Summit in Shenzhen

1 of 2
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomes US President Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders Summit in Shenzhen, China November 18, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria

By Simon Lewis and Jonathan Landay

WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Republican lawmakers on Wednesday urged President Donald Trump to again press Chinese leader Xi Jinping to free two Americans designated as wrongfully detained, ‌as well as political prisoners, when the two meet in Shenzhen on Thursday.

Advocates for the ‌Americans, Youlin Chen and Min Zin, say they expect Trump to raise their cases with Xi.

Advertisement

John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee ​on China, Robert Aderholt, chairman of the House Values Action Team, and Chris Smith, co-chairman of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China, issued the statement. Seventeen other House Republicans co-signed it.

The lawmakers said the two men were held on "baseless suspicions" of endangering national security. They cited the July release of Pastor Ezra Jin as an example of ‌diplomacy producing results and called for other ⁠detainees, including Hong Kong media mogul Jimmy Lai and Uyghur economist Ilham Tohti, to be freed.

"They should all be released immediately," the lawmakers said.

Responding to the statement, a ⁠US official said, "Resolving the wrongful detentions of US citizens is always a top priority for the president."

The wrongfully detained designation makes the pair's release a top US priority.

US officials and advocates for the detained pair say China has not ​engaged on ​the cases, despite Trump raising Chen's case at a ​meeting with Xi in May and both men's cases ‌in September.

A Chinese Embassy spokesperson said: "China is a country governed by the rule of law. Its judicial authorities handle cases in accordance with the law, and there is no such thing as so-called wrongful detention."

Min Zin, a researcher on Myanmar, was detained during a visit to southwest China in June. China's Foreign Ministry said the American citizen was suspected of spying and endangering Chinese national security.

Chen is a Chinese-born seismologist whose published work ‌on the seismographic signatures of North Korean nuclear tests was ​US-funded. He was arrested at Beijing's international airport on November 5, ​2024, as he prepared to fly home. ​Chinese authorities charged him with espionage on May 1, 2025.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio ‌has designated both men as wrongfully detained.

The State ​Department last month added a "D" ​indicator to its China travel advisory, warning of the risk of wrongful detention. It could raise the risk level of its travel advisory for China if progress is not made.

Eric Lebson, chief strategy ​officer of Global Reach, an advocacy ‌group working with Chen's family, said it was "uncharacteristic of the Chinese government to not engage on ​resolving matters of this type after two discussions about them at the presidential level."

(Reporting by ​Simon Lewis and Jonathan Landay; Editing by Sonali Paul)

data.title: Republican senator blocks Trump's judicial nominee as Democrats prepare to take over
data.description:
Republican Senator Cornyn blocks Trump judicial nominee in Texas

By Nate Raymond and David Morgan
Wed, November 18, 2026 at 7:17 PM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Nate Raymond and David Morgan

WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's efforts to secure Senate confirmation of as many conservative judges as possible before Democrats take control of the chamber suffered a setback on Wednesday after ‌a Republican senator blocked one of his nominees from advancing.

Outgoing Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas withheld support for US ‌Department of Justice official T. Elliot Gaiser to appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee for a hearing on Wednesday where it could take up his nomination to be a ​federal judge in Dallas.

Advertisement

Cornyn's decision not to return a so-called blue slip backing Gaiser marked the latest instance of a Republican senator not supporting a White House-backed judicial nominee in their home state during the lame-duck session before Democrats take control of the Senate on January 3.

"He's not from Texas," Cornyn told Reuters. "He has no trial experience, and the White House was trying to jam him down our throat without adequate ‌vetting for a lifetime job."

A White House official ⁠in a statement said it expects all of Trump's judicial nominees to be confirmed by year's end.

Senators traditionally help choose nominees for vacancies on federal courts in their states. By Senate custom, they can effectively veto ⁠trial court nominees they oppose in their states by refusing to return a blue slip, a form used to signal support.

Trump nominated Gaiser, 37, to a seat on the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas after the election.

The former Ohio solicitor general previously clerked for conservative US ​Supreme ​Court Justice Samuel Alito and currently heads the Justice Department's Office of ​Legal Counsel, a key unit that has frequently signed ‌off on the legality of his administration's actions.

Cornyn, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, during Wednesday's hearing expressed support for Trump's decision to separately nominate Texas Supreme Court Justice James Sullivan to serve as a federal judge after he was defeated by a Democrat in the recent election.

But Cornyn has been pushing for the White House to pick someone else for the seat Gaiser was nominated to fill, recommending instead former federal prosecutor Steve Fahey of Texas.

"And the White House now seems to ‌be showing some interest in that," Cornyn said in an interview.

Republican Senator Ted ​Cruz of Texas, who supports Gaiser, in a statement warned that the White ​House has indicated that it would be "impossible for a brand-new ​nominee to complete the FBI background check fast enough to be confirmed."

"If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not ‌move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay ​the price because it will effectively ​give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity," Cruz said.

Two of Trump's other judicial nominees similarly ran into resistance from Republican senators in their home states after the midterm elections.

The White House on November 10 rescinded ​US District Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the ‌8th US Circuit Court of Appeals and nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland in his place following opposition ​from Arkansas' Republican senator. Hiland appeared at Wednesday's hearing with six other nominees.

(Reporting by Nate Raymond in Boston and ​David Morgan in Washington; Editing by Bill Berkrot and Alistair Bell)

data.title: U.S. and Venezuela agree to share military intelligence after Maduro's capture
data.description:
US and Venezuela sign a deal to reestablish military ties, Hegseth says in visit to Caracas

JORGE RUEDA, KONSTANTIN TOROPIN and REGINA GARCIA CANO
Updated Wed, November 18, 2026 at 4:22 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Venezuela US Hegseth

1 of 3
In this photo released by Miraflores presidential press office, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, meets with Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez at Miraflores presidential palace in Caracas, Venezuela, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. (Miraflores presidential press office, via AP) (Miraflores presidential press office via AP)

CARACAS, Venezuela (AP) — The United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties that will range from conducting joint training to intelligence sharing, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday in Caracas while visiting the South American nation's interim leaders.

Hegseth touted how U.S. forces in January captured then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, telling an audience of diplomats and military officials from both countries that now Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner."

He also praised the "close cooperation" with acting President Delcy Rodríguez that allowed officials "to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all," in a reference to drug traffickers.

Advertisement

Hegseth's visit, the latest in a series of stops in Venezuela by members of President Donald Trump's Cabinet, underscores efforts by the U.S. administration to deepen its influence in the South American country. Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.

Hegseth praises Trump's Venezuela oil deal

The Pentagon chief praised the energy deal by referencing another major military action by the Trump administration this year — the Iran war. The conflict has disrupted global energy supplies through a critical waterway in the Persian Gulf, raising gasoline prices and contributing to the Republican Party's severe losses in this month's midterm elections.

The Venezuela oil deal "makes the Strait of Hormuz a non-factor for the Western Hemisphere," Hegseth said at the U.S. embassy in Caracas.

In the meeting with Hegseth, Rodríguez asserted that the deal enables "the energy development of our nations" and "benefits both the people of the United States and the people of Venezuela."

Among those in attendance for Hegseth's speech was Alejandro Betancourt, the owner of North American Blue Energy Partners, the second-largest oil operator in Venezuela. The U.S. government and Betancourt's company entered into the ambitious agreement to tap Venezuela's vast oil reserves.

Both the Interior and Energy secretaries also visited Venezuela earlier this year and focused their efforts on tapping its oil reserves and critical minerals. The head of U.S. military operations in Latin America, Gen. Francis Donovan of U.S. Southern Command, also has met interim authorities in Venezuela at least twice this year.

Few details provided on the US-Venezuela military agreement

Hegseth offered few specifics on what the military agreement would entail, beyond saying that the two countries' militaries would be "training together, partnering together, sharing intelligence, more defense equipment and capabilities together."

Speaking separately, Rodríguez said she hoped the countries' military cooperation "can be brought to its highest possible level" to allow them to "address common threats."

Hegseth pointed to Venezuela partnering with the U.S. "to recover its territory from narco-terrorist networks." The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.

The development comes as the U.S. military has been expanding its attention on the region since Trump's return to the White House last year, with the Republican president promising to focus more on the Western Hemisphere and battle Latin American drug cartels.

To try to stem the flow of narcotics into the U.S. and the scourge of fatal overdoses, American forces have been attacking what the Trump administration says are boats smuggling drugs in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. At least 240 people have been killed since the administration began targeting those it calls "narco-terrorists" in September 2025, although U.S. officials have released little evidence publicly to support claims the vessels were carrying drugs or that they have made an impact on the availability of drugs in the country.

Hegseth also used his speech to boast about the military operation that seized Maduro, calling it "the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America" that "lasted just 48 minutes."

"America's best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours," he added.

But Venezuela's ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge.

Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader "predicted," the operation ended with "no war, yes, peace."

Uncertainty about Venezuela's political future

Hegseth's visit also comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.

Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro's capture and despite the fact that her court-allowed term expired in July, she has continued to function as Venezuela's head of state.

Hegseth praised her leadership and thanked her for "working closely and pragmatically and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela."

Meanwhile, opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the "safe" return of the politician was the result of "reconciliation talks" supported by the U.S., which he considered "the best opportunity" Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.

The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House's decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela's oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.

___

Toropin reported from Washington. Associated Press writer Ben Finley in Washington contributed to this report.

data.title: Trump to hold one-on-one talks with Putin on the sidelines of Asia summit
data.description:
Trump administration

Trump to hold one-on-one with Putin on the sidelines of Asia summit

A U.S. official confirmed that the two leaders would hold a bilateral meeting despite indications from White House officials that Trump and Putin would not meet separately.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Nov. 18, 2026, 10:39 AM EST / Updated Nov. 18, 2026, 11:08 AM EST
By Monica Alba and Megan Brand

President Donald Trump will hold a one-on-one meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday, a U.S. official confirmed, marking the leaders’ first in-person meeting in over a year.

The bilateral meeting was not initially on Trump’s schedule for his Asia trip. The president was already scheduled to hold a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, where the leaders plan to discuss nuclear disarmament, the Iran war, trade and, Trump said Monday, Russia’s war with Ukraine.

The Kremlin had said ahead of the U.S.’ confirmation that the two leaders would be meeting one-on-one.

The White House has not released information about the agenda for the bilateral meeting, which comes as major attacks continue in the Ukraine war with no end in sight. Trump’s meetings with the leaders of China and Russia — both U.S. adversaries — marks his administration’s continued shift away from traditional alliances and unconventional approach to diplomacy.

A senior U.S. official previously told reporters that while the president intended to discuss Iran with Xi and Putin during their trilateral meeting, he did not plan to focus on the war in Ukraine. The official said last week that “it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there” with China.

Trump and Putin previously met face-to-face in Alaska in August 2025. That summit ended without an agreement to end the war in Ukraine, something Trump has been pursuing since he began his second term.

Trump continued to express optimism about ending the war after the in-person meeting in Alaska did not lead to any ceasefire or breakthrough.

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he believed Putin was “backing down a little bit” in the war in Ukraine.

“I think he could be tougher,” Trump said. “I think he could be a lot tougher, frankly. I think he’s backing down.”

Russia, however, has continued striking Ukraine with missiles and drones in the lead up to the meeting. Separately, on Tuesday, Ukraine damaged a key bridge that links the occupied Crimean Peninsula with Russia.

Trump repeatedly said during his 2024 presidential campaign that he could quickly end the war between Russia and Ukraine.

“I will get it settled before I even become president,” Trump said during a presidential debate.

As Trump heads into the second half of his final term, the war is entering its fifth year.
